Discrete Event Simulation Course Syllabus
This syllabus defines a 12-week course in discrete event simulation delivered across 24
sessions and 48 teaching hours. It sets out learning outcomes, the weekly schedule,
laboratory expectations, assessment weightings and academic conduct rules. Students
learn to model queueing and service systems, build event calendars, validate models
against observations and report findings with appropriate uncertainty language. All figures
in this document are simulated planning values for instructional design purposes.

1 Course Design and Learning Outcomes
The course is organized around a build-measure-explain cycle. Each week pairs a short
conceptual lecture with a hands-on laboratory, so students encounter theory and
implementation together. By the end, learners should be able to translate a process
description into an event-driven model, justify input distributions, and distinguish simulated
outputs from causal claims about real systems. Instructors review drafts within 5 working
days to keep feedback timely.
Supporting records are presented in Table 2.
1.1 Weekly Topic Sequence
Topics progress from foundational mechanics to interpretation. Early weeks cover event
scheduling, random number generation and entity flow; middle weeks address input
modeling, warm-up periods and replication; later weeks focus on validation, sensitivity
analysis and communicating results. The sequence assumes no prior simulation software
experience but expects comfort with basic probability and programming constructs such as
loops and records.
Supporting records are presented in Table 1.
1.1.1 Event Scheduling and Queue Mechanics
This unit examines the event calendar as the engine of any discrete event model. Students
implement a priority queue of events, trace entity arrivals and departures, and observe how
service discipline changes waiting behavior. Laboratory exercises require a trace log
showing each event time and state change, so that instructors can verify understanding of
simultaneity and tie-breaking rules rather than only final averages.
1.1.2 Random Variates and Input Modeling
Students generate variates from uniform, exponential and empirical distributions, then fit
candidate distributions to provided arrival and service records. The unit stresses

documenting assumptions and testing fit rather than selecting a distribution by
convenience. Exercises ask learners to compare fitted models against held-out observations
and to explain, in plain language, why a good fit does not by itself prove the underlying
process behaves that way.
1.2 Validation and Sensitivity Checks
Table 1: Weekly topic sequence with conceptual and laboratory emphasis
Validation activities compare model behavior with recorded system observations and
structured expert review. Students perform face validation, trace-driven checks and simple
sensitivity sweeps on key parameters. The unit emphasizes reporting ranges and caveats
alongside point estimates, and it explicitly separates what the simulation observed from
what may be inferred about the real system. Deliverables include a validation log with
decisions and rejected alternatives.
Supporting records are presented in Figure 1.
Figure 1: Validation checks and the evidence each check produces
1.2.1 Trace-Driven Validation Exercises
Students replay recorded system traces through their models and compare simulated
outputs against observed values. Exercises use a sample of 240 observations drawn from 4
sites across 2022 to 2025, giving a realistic basis for discrepancy analysis. Teams document
each mismatch, classify its likely source, and decide whether to adjust logic, parameters, or
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT | RESEARCH PROTOTYPE
accept the deviation with a stated caveat in the validation log.
1.2.2 Sensitivity Sweeps and Reporting Ranges
Sensitivity sessions vary key inputs across plausible bounds and record how outputs
respond, such as output values moving from 79.55 to 119.76 and costs from 51.71 to
77.84. Students summarize results as ranges with caveats rather than single point
estimates, and they practice separating what the simulation observed from what may be
inferred about the real system when presenting findings.
2 Assessment and Laboratory Schedule
Assessment combines laboratory submissions, a midterm modeling task and a final project
with a written report and short presentation. Weights and due dates appear in the schedule
table below. Late work is accepted within 2 days of the deadline with a documented
penalty, and regrade requests must be filed within 5 days of feedback release. The final
project replaces a traditional closed-book examination.
Supporting records are presented in Figure 3.
2.1 Assessment Components and Weightings
Each component targets a distinct skill: laboratories test implementation discipline, the
midterm tests modeling judgment under time pressure, and the final project tests
end-to-end reasoning from problem framing to reported conclusions. Rubrics are published
at the start of term. Students receive formative feedback on at least two laboratory
submissions before the midterm, ensuring they can adjust before higher-stakes work
begins.
2.1.1 Laboratory Submissions
Laboratories are submitted as reproducible scripts plus a short memo. The memo must
state model scope, input assumptions, replication count and observed output ranges, using
the reporting template distributed in week one. Graders check that scripts run without
manual edits and that memos avoid overclaiming. Partial credit is available for correct
mechanics with incomplete interpretation, reflecting the course emphasis on both building
and explaining.
2.1.2 Final Project and Presentation
The final project asks teams to model a chosen service process, validate it against supplied
or collected observations, and present findings with explicit limitations. Presentations are
brief and followed by questions on assumptions and alternative explanations. Teams must
show at least one sensitivity check and one rejected modeling choice, demonstrating that
conclusions were tested rather than asserted. A shared repository preserves scripts and
logs for review.

2.2 Policies and Support Resources
The course follows institutional policies on academic integrity, accessibility and respectful
conduct. Students may collaborate on conceptual discussion but must submit individually
authored laboratory memos unless a project is explicitly team-based. Office hours run
weekly, and a discussion forum supports asynchronous questions with responses typically
within 2 days. Accommodation requests are handled through the standard institutional
process and kept confidential.
